en: The Sūtra on the Eight Precepts Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the layman Juqu Jingsheng of the Song Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In the Jeta Grove,
at that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now proclaim the noble eightfold fast."
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now speak.
They replied, "So be it, World-Honored One!"
At that time, those bhikṣus received the instruction from the Buddha.
The World-Honored One addressed them, saying:
"In this regard, bhikṣus!"
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has faith wishes to know the Noble Eightfold Observance of the Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-śīla), one should instruct them as follows:

"Just as an Arhat, for as long as life lasts, does not kill living beings nor incite others to kill; being free from resentment and harboring a sense of shame and remorse, they possess a heart of loving-kindness and compassion for all sentient beings."

I, whose surname is [Name] and whose given name is [Name], have been instructed by an Arhat; from this day forward, I shall no longer take life according to my own desires, harboring no heart of resentment and always maintaining a sense of shame and remorse, possessing a mind of loving-kindness that takes pity on all sentient beings.
Just as an arhat, for the remainder of his life, does not steal and delights in giving, nor does he instruct others to steal, but always finds joy in secluded places;

so too am I, [name] by word and [name] by title, instructed by the arhat: according to my own desire, I shall no longer steal, but shall always cherish the practice of giving and delight in dwelling in seclusion.
Just as an Arhat, for as long as life lasts, does not engage in impure conduct, but constantly cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*), remaining pure and undefiled while finding joy therein;
so too am I, [name], instructed by an Arhat, that from this day forward I shall no longer engage in sexual misconduct, but remain pure and undefiled.
Just as an arhat, for as long as life lasts, refrains from false speech, always acting with discernment and truthfulness—being most honored and most noble, and esteemed by all elders and the world.

Thus, I, whose name is so-and-so, having been instructed by that Arhat, shall from this day forward never again speak falsely, nor shall I instruct others to practice falsehood; I shall act with careful discernment and, for the sake of the World-Honored One, shall not engage in lying.

Just as an Arhat does not drink alcohol, so too I, who am called [surname] and named [given name], from this day forward shall not drink alcohol according to my own will, nor shall I instruct others to drink alcohol.
Just as an Arhat, for the duration of his life, does not violate the fast and eats at the proper time,

so too I, [name] by my given name [surname], for one day and one night, according to my desire, shall likewise not violate the fast, nor shall I instruct others to violate the fast, and I shall eat at the proper time.
Just as an Arhat, for as long as life lasts, does not sit upon high or luxurious beds,
so too do I, who am called by such-and-such a name, for one day and one night, refrain from sitting upon high or broad beds, nor shall I instruct others to sit upon them.
Just as an arhat, for the remainder of his life, does not practice singing, dancing, or theatrical entertainment, nor does he wear ornamental patterns, apply perfumes, or smear scents upon his body;
so too, for this one day and night, I shall not practice singing, dancing, or theatrical entertainment, nor shall I wear ornamental patterns, apply perfumes, or smear scents upon my body.

"Practicing the noble eightfold fast in this manner, the merit within these eight precepts is immeasurable; one cannot say that there are only so many blessings, so many merits, or so many rewards of fortune. Such a multitude of blessings is beyond calculation."

"O monks! It is as if five great flowing rivers all converge in one place—namely, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Sindhu, the Aciravatī, and the Mahī. The extent of the water where those rivers flow is immeasurable; one cannot say there is such-and-such a quantity of water, or such-and-such a number of jars of water, or such-and-such a number of thousands or hundreds of thousands of jars of water."

In this way, the merit of the noble eightfold fast is immeasurable; one cannot say that it possesses such-and-such merit, such-and-such virtue, or such-and-such retribution, for this great merit is beyond calculation.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus ends the *Buddha-bhāṣita-aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-sūtra*.
